title: Resolving the Structural Origin of Lattice Oxygen Release across Scales in Practical Lithium‐Manganese‐Rich Electrodes
content:
Gas measurements capture only the collective outcome of reactions across an electrode, leaving the structural origin of oxygen release hidden. This work maps manganese reduction, a fingerprint of oxygen release, from electrode to grain by combining online mass spectrometry with multi‐scale X‐ray and electron microscopy. Grain‐facet exposure, not electrode or particle structure, emerges as its key structural descriptor.








ABSTRACT
Gas evolution from lattice oxygen release is a major obstacle to deployment of high‐energy‐density cathodes, yet its structural origin within dense electrodes remains challenging to resolve across multiple length scales. This difficulty arises because gas evolution is the collective outcome of oxygen release from numerous grains and particles, whose environments can vary across electrode, secondary‐particle, and grain scales. Here, by integrating online electrochemical mass spectrometry with synchrotron X‐ray and electron microscopy, this study resolves the spatial origin of O2 evolution through mapping Mn reduction, a chemical fingerprint of oxygen release, across four orders of magnitude in length scale. Two lithium‐manganese‐rich layered oxide (LMR) electrodes that vary only in secondary‐particle size are employed as a model system, and their O2 evolution differs twofold. Spatially resolving Mn oxidation state distribution reveals no detectable Mn‐reduction gradient across the electrode thickness or within particles, indicating that the difference does not originate from electrode‐ or particle‐scale heterogeneity. Instead, frontal facets (lithium‐intercalation planes) of grains exhibit deeper Mn reduction and surface reconstruction than lateral facets, consistent with favorable oxygen vacancy formation and migration. O2 evolution matches after frontal‐facet area normalization, identifying frontal‐facet exposure as a key structural descriptor for O2 evolution in these practical LMR electrodes.
journal: Wiley: Advanced Energy Materials: Table of Contents
summary: Maps Mn reduction as a fingerprint of O2 release from electrode to grain scale (four orders of magnitude). It finds no electrode- or particle-scale gradient. Frontal (Li-intercalation-plane) facets reduce more deeply, and normalizing by frontal-facet area reconciles the twofold difference in O2 evolution between the two electrodes. This gives a quantitative structural descriptor.
technique: OEMS + multiscale synchrotron X-ray spectro-microscopy (XANES mapping) + STEM/EELS

title:
Discovering Underpotentially
Deposited Crystalline
Sodium Metal Nanoparticles on the Surface of Hard Carbon Anodes
content:
Abstract
Sodium-ion batteries are attractive candidates for low-cost and scalable energy storage in which hard carbon (HC) anodes are used. However, sodium (Na) metal plating in HC anodes at voltages above the plating potential remains a critical problem. The location and spatial distribution of crystalline sodium (c-Na) metal nanoparticles, the clusters associated with Na storage in HCs, are important for understanding this underpotential plating behavior but remain unclear. Here, we implement a cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and electron tomography (cryo-ET) workflow that directly localizes c-Na metal clusters in sodiated HC samples: cryo-ET maps nanoscale three-dimensional (3D) distributions, while cryo-EM resolves local structure and chemistry. Our workflow reveals that c-Na metal clusters reside predominantly on the surfaces or near surfaces of individual HC particles. This finding challenges existing interpretations in the literature that locate the c-Na metal clusters within closed nanopores in the bulk of the HC, presumably because prior characterization using nonimaging techniques and two-dimensional (2D) projection images associated with traditional transmission electron microscopy (TEM) lacks the spatial 3D information necessary to resolve the full spatial distribution. Our discovery is an important step toward explaining the underpotential plating phenomenon of Na metal in HC anodes, suggesting that particle-level surface and near-surface interfaces are relevant targets to mitigate plating alongside bulk-pore, electrode, and electrolyte/interphase design.
journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society ASAP
summary: Cryo-ET localizes crystalline Na metal clusters in sodiated hard carbon in 3D, finding them on or near particle surfaces rather than in closed bulk nanopores. This contradicts the prevailing pore-filling picture and redirects mitigation of underpotential plating toward particle surfaces and interfaces.

title: Operando X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy Reveals Oxide Solid Electrolyte Stability against Electrochemically Plated Lithium
content:
Abstract
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) has revealed many possible Li-induced interfacial reactions in solid-state electrolytes (SSEs), but most in situ studies form Li|electrolyte interfaces through non-electrochemical Li deposition, including evaporation, sputtering, or electron-beam-induced deposition. These routes may introduce additional energy that activates reaction pathways not accessed during electrochemical Li plating. Here, we use lab-based operando XPS to directly evaluate oxide solid-state electrolyte stability during electrochemical Li formation. Using this approach, we find sharply different responses for two representative oxide SSEs: NASICON-type Li1+xAlxTi2–x(PO4)3 (LATP) is reduced upon Li plating, forming a Li+/Ti3+-rich mixed-conducting interphase that partially relaxes through coupled ionic–electronic redistribution, whereas garnet-type Li7La3Zr2O12 (LLZO) shows no spectroscopically resolvable Zr or La reduction. This work represents the first direct operando XPS evaluation of SSE stability against electrochemically plated Li metal.
summary: Plates Li electrochemically inside the XPS, avoiding the artefacts of evaporation or sputtering. It shows LATP is reduced to a Li+/Ti3+ mixed-conducting interphase that partly relaxes, while LLZO shows no resolvable Zr or La reduction. This resolves a known inconsistency in the in situ XPS literature.
technique: lab-based operando XPS with electrochemical Li plating

title: Operando Magnetometry Decodes Space‐Charge Storage in the Solid‐Electrolyte Interphase
content:
Operando magnetometry tracks reversible magnetic changes in Fe3C‐based electrodes during cycling. Combined electrochemical and interfacial analyses support an electron‐ion job‐sharing storage mechanism between Fe3C and inorganic‐rich SEI at the electrode interface. This work reveals that the SEI can contribute to interfacial charge storage, offering a new perspective for understanding and designing high‐rate energy‐storage electrodes.








ABSTRACT
The solid‐electrolyte interphase (SEI) is central to ion transport and electrode stability in lithium‐ion batteries (LIBs), yet how charges dynamically distribute and migrate across the SEI/electrode interface during cycling remains elusive. Here, we couple operando magnetometry with an Fe3C magnetic probe to track real‑time charge migration across this electrochemical interface. By further integrating operando ambient‐pressure x‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy (AP‐XPS) with multiscale structural and chemical characterizations, we provide converging evidence that supports SEI‐centered space‐charge storage at the electrode interface. This interfacial space‐charge layer delivers an additional ≈236 mAh g−1 within 0.01–1.4 V. The inorganic‐rich SEI forms efficient ionic pathways, whereas Fe3C accommodates spin‑polarized electrons, enabling decoupled ionic and electronic storage across the interface. Additionally, the lithium‐ion hybrid capacitors assembled with the Fe3C NP@C electrode deliver an energy density of 98.9 Wh kg−1 at a power density of 20,000 W kg−1 together with sustained long‐term stability. These findings expand the functional role of the SEI and show that operando magnetometry can serve as a sensitive real‐time probe of magnetically coupled interfacial processes in the Fe3C‐based and related magnetic systems.
journal: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
summary: Uses operando magnetometry with Fe3C as a magnetic probe to follow reversible charge storage at the SEI/electrode interface. Operando AP-XPS supports an SEI-centred space-charge mechanism, giving about 236 mAh/g extra capacity. The method is new and transferable, but space-charge storage claims in conversion-type electrodes are still debated and the evidence is indirect.

title: Demonstrating the Generality of Kerr-Gated Raman Spectroscopy Measurements of High Charge States in Graphitic Electrodes for Li-Ion Batteries
content:
Abstract
Herein, the systematic application of the Kerr-gated Raman spectroscopy technique to track lithium intercalation into Li-ion graphite electrodes is reported under different operando, in situ, and ex situ experimental conditions with different graphitic electrode materials and electrolyte material formulations, through multiple cycles. The results revealed a broad generality of (i) the capability of the technique to resolve the characteristic G-band of graphite electrodes even at high charge states (high states of lithiation) and (ii) the sensitivity of the shift in the observed G-band to the state of electrochemical lithiation at high charge states during the transition from stage 2 to stage 1 (0.5 ≤ x ≤1 for LixC6). The shifted G-band was observed in highly lithiated electrodes comprising different graphite sources and conventional Li-ion-type electrolyte formulations and was further replicated using a noncommercial ionic liquid-based electrolyte formulation. Additionally, the persistence of the G-band (and the related shift as a function of charge) was replicated in many ex situ samples across 10 cycles, further evidencing the potential of this technique as a diagnostic tool to track high states of charge in cycled graphite-based negative electrodes for Li-ion batteries.
summary: Kerr-gating suppresses fluorescence and lets the graphite G-band be resolved at high lithiation (stage 2→1, 0.5≤x≤1), where conventional Raman fails. The paper shows the G-band shift tracks state of lithiation across graphite sources, carbonate and ionic-liquid electrolytes, and 10 cycles. The work is a generality demonstration, not spatial imaging.

title: Operando  Raman Spectroscopy-Guided 24-Hour Aging Assessment of Activated Carbon Positive Electrodes for Lithium-Ion Capacitors
content:
Abstract
While high-power lithium-ion capacitors (LICs) with high energy density emerge as promising pulse-/peak-power solutions for AI data centers, their long-term viability remains severely hindered by the degradation of the activated carbon (AC) positive electrode. To evaluate this aging behavior, we propose a 24-h high-voltage cycling (HVC) protocol integrated with operando Raman spectroscopy, demonstrating that the turning point in the D1 band can serve as a sensitive indicator of corrosion severity. During the early-stage HVC aging, cathode–electrolyte interphase (CEI) formation and gas evolution passivate defect-related Raman signals, narrowing the D1 band. As aging proceeds, carbon corrosion becomes dominant and broadens the D1 band. By validating this approach across various ACs, we establish a direct correlation between an earlier structural turning point and accelerated capacity decay, thereby uncovering carbon aging mechanisms and offering an unprecedented, rapid diagnostic technique for capacitor-type materials.
summary: Operando Raman of AC cathodes in lithium-ion capacitors under high-voltage cycling finds a turning point in D1 band width. It narrows first as CEI and gas passivate defects, then broadens with corrosion. An earlier turning point correlates with faster capacity decay, giving a 24-h aging diagnostic. The work is spectroscopic but not spatially resolved.

title: In Situ Visualizing the Electric‐Field‐Driven Assembly of Gradient Carbon Dot Hydrogel Electrolytes for Stable Zinc Battery
content:
Carbon dots with phenolic hydroxyl groups are engineered to enable electric‐field‐driven electrophoretic migration in hydrogel electrolytes. An operando electrochemical–confocal platform directly visualizes their dynamic redistribution and interfacial enrichment. This process induces a gradient structure that homogenizes the electric field, regulates Zn2+ flux, suppresses parasitic reactions, and significantly enhances the electrochemical stability of aqueous zinc‐ion batteries.








ABSTRACT
Aqueous zinc‐ion batteries (AZIBs) have seen increasing use of carbon dots (CDs) as functional additives; however, their interfacial regulation mechanisms remain unclear due to the lack of direct in situ visualization under realistic conditions. In this study, we develop an operando electrochemical–confocal coupled platform that enables real‐time tracking of fluorescent CDs under an applied electric field. Using this system, we directly visualize the electrophoretic migration and interfacial enrichment of CDs, providing clear evidence of their roles in electric‐field modulation and Zn2+ flux regulation. Guided by this insight, a gradient‐structured poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) hydrogel electrolyte (2PVA@CDs) is in situ constructed via electric‐field‐driven assembly. Zn||Zn symmetric cells with 2PVA@CDs exhibit ultralong cycling stability over 6500 h at 1 mA cm−2 and 1 mAh cm−2, and stable operation for 900 h at 85% depth of discharge. Combined experiments, finite element simulations, and density functional theory calculations reveal that CDs homogenize the interfacial electric field, regulate Zn2+ flux, reduce the nucleation energy barrier, and suppress hydrogen evolution, thereby enhancing interfacial stability and overall electrochemical performance. This work clarifies the mechanistic role of CDs and establishes a general operando visualization strategy for functional additives in metal batteries.
journal: Wiley: Advanced Materials: Table of Contents
summary: Couples a confocal fluorescence platform with an electrochemical cell to track fluorescent carbon dots migrating electrophoretically in a hydrogel electrolyte and enriching at the Zn interface. The visualization is used to build a gradient electrolyte. The mechanism rationale still leans on FEM and DFT, and the additive is zinc-specific.

title: Electrochemically In Situ Formed Inverse‐Honeycomb Local Ordering for Low‐Voltage‐Hysteresis Oxygen Redox in Na/Li Layered Oxide Cathodes
content:
An O3‐type NaLi0.2Ni0.2Mn0.6O2 cathode undergoes electrochemically induced reconstruction of inverse‐honeycomb ordering in the alkali layer during deep desodiation. The reconstructed superstructure suppresses Ni‐centered ligand‐to‐metal charge transfer, preserves more high‐voltage cationic‐redox contribution, and reduces delayed low‐voltage oxygen reduction, thereby mitigating voltage hysteresis and voltage decay while maintaining high reversible capacity.








ABSTRACT
In oxygen‐redox cathodes, voltage hysteresis largely arises as oxygen redox generally proceeds with electrochemical reactions followed by chemical reactions that normally drive asymmetrical charge and discharge pathways. Although different superstructures, such as ribbon and mesh units, were intentionally introduced to mitigate voltage hysteresis, those structures remain as model compounds that can hardly be implemented in real‐world applications. Here, inspired by the classical Li‐rich layered Li[Li0.2Ni0.2Mn0.6]O2, we design a new O3‐type sodium layered oxide, NaLi0.2Ni0.2Mn0.6O2, that delivers 205.2 mA h g−1 with reversible oxygen redox but shows mitigated voltage hysteresis and suppressed voltage decay. Atomic‐resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy reveals that deep desodiation reconstruts an addtional inverse‐honeycomb superstructure in the alkali layer, which is retained after discharge and extended cycling. Li analogues prepared via (electro)chemical ion‐exchange reactions from pristine and charged‐state Na precursors further reveal the critical role of this inverse‐honeycomb ordering in suppressing voltage hysteresis. Thermal relaxation experiments combined with spectroscopic studies show that inverse‐honeycomb ordering suppresses Ni‐centered ligand‐to‐metal charge transfer associated with chemical relaxation, allowing the reduction process to proceed from a nonequilibrium state, thereby mitigating voltage hysteresis. Our study provides practical significance in this newly designed Na compound NaLi0.2Ni0.2Mn0.6O2 by taking advantage of in situ formation of inverse‐honeycomb ordering.
journal: Wiley: Angewandte Chemie International Edition: Table of Contents
summary: Atomic-resolution STEM shows that deep desodiation of NaLi0.2Ni0.2Mn0.6O2 forms an inverse-honeycomb superstructure in the alkali layer. Comparing Li analogues made by ion exchange from pristine and charged precursors, plus thermal relaxation and spectroscopy, ties this ordering to suppressed Ni-centred ligand-to-metal charge transfer and lower voltage hysteresis. The evidence is mostly ex situ.
technique: atomic-resolution STEM, ex situ spectroscopy, thermal relaxation, ion-exchange
